Fehling's solution is alkaline Cu²⁺ complexed with tartrate. A reducing sugar reduces the Cu²⁺
to Cu⁺, giving a red precipitate of Cu₂O.
For that to happen the sugar must be able to open into a free aldehyde (or an α-hydroxy ketone
that can tautomerise to one).
Glucose is an aldohexose. In solution its ring opens to expose a free –CHO group, so it reduces
Fehling's ✓
Sucrose cannot. Both of its anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic link, so no open-chain
aldehyde can form — it is a non-reducing sugar.
Fats are esters of glycerol and fatty acids, and proteins are polymers of amino acids; neither
has a free aldehyde group.
∴ glucose.

kcet|Chemistry|2016|46||0|0.s:
Think about what bounds the liquid state from each side at ordinary pressure.
Below the melting point the substance is solid — the particles are locked in a lattice.
Above the boiling point it is a gas — the particles have enough energy to escape completely.
So at a given pressure the liquid occupies the band between those two temperatures, and that
is the band the question is after.
The wider thermodynamic statement, if you include pressure as a variable, is that a liquid can
exist only between the triple point and the critical point: below the triple point the solid
sublimes straight to vapour, and above the critical temperature no amount of pressure will
liquefy the gas, because the distinction between the two phases disappears.
∴ between the melting and boiling points.

Bohr's model gives the energy of the electron in the nth orbit of a hydrogen-like atom as
Eₙ = −2π²mZ²e⁴/(n²h²)
Putting the constants in and setting Z = 1 for hydrogen:
Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV
The n² in the denominator is the part to remember, and the sign matters too.
The energy is negative because the electron is bound: zero is defined as the electron free and
at rest, so any bound state must lie below it.
Check: n = 1 gives −13.6 eV, the ground state, and the energy needed to remove that electron
is 13.6 eV, which is hydrogen's measured ionisation energy ✓
As n grows the levels crowd towards zero, which is why spectral lines converge.
∴ Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV.

Find the statement that is false.
(1) True — vulcanisation heats rubber with sulphur, forming –S–S– cross-links between the
chains. These stop the chains sliding past each other, so the rubber becomes harder, stronger
and far less sticky.
(4) True — natural rubber is a 1,4-addition polymer of isoprene (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene).
(2) False — natural rubber is **cis**-1,4-polyisoprene, not trans. The cis double bonds put a kink
in the chain, so the molecules cannot pack closely; the coiled chains stretch out and spring back,
which is exactly where the elasticity comes from.
The trans isomer of the same polymer is gutta-percha, and because its chains *can* pack neatly
it is hard and non-elastic.
(3) is loosely worded — Buna-S is made from buta**diene** and styrene, not butene — but (2) is
the statement the examiner marks as untrue.
∴ statement (2) is not true.

A polyamide has the amide link –CO–NH– repeating along its backbone.
Nylon-6,6 is made by condensing hexamethylenediamine with adipic acid. The –NH₂ of one
reacts with the –COOH of the other, losing water and leaving an amide bond ✓
The two 6s count the carbons in each monomer.
Terylene (Dacron) condenses ethylene glycol with terephthalic acid, so its link is an ester,
–CO–O–. It is a poly**ester**.
Polythene is an addition polymer of ethene — just a carbon chain, no functional link at all.
Buna-S is an addition copolymer of butadiene and styrene, again pure hydrocarbon.
Note that nylons, having N–H bonds, hydrogen bond strongly between chains, which is why they
make such strong fibres.
∴ Nylon-6,6.
kcet|Chemistry|2016|53||0|0:
The two strands of DNA are held together by hydrogen bonds between the bases, and the
pairing is fixed by geometry: a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, so that every rung of the
ladder is the same width.
Purines: adenine (A) and guanine (G) — two fused rings.
Pyrimidines: thymine (T) and cytosine (C) — one ring.
The pairs are:
A with T, held by **two** hydrogen bonds
G with C, held by **three** hydrogen bonds
A–G would be purine with purine, too wide; T–C pyrimidine with pyrimidine, too narrow. Neither
fits the double helix, which rules out options (2), (3) and (4).
Because G–C has the extra hydrogen bond, DNA rich in G and C needs a higher temperature to
separate its strands.
(In RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine and pairs with adenine.)
∴ A–T and G–C.

Sort the four by what they are used for.
Equanil (meprobamate) is a tranquilliser — a neurologically active drug used to treat anxiety,
stress and mild depression ✓ Other examples are veronal, valium and chlordiazepoxide.
Naproxen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory and analgesic, in the same family as aspirin and
ibuprofen — it relieves pain, it does not calm the nervous system.
Tetracycline is a broad-spectrum antibiotic, which acts on bacteria rather than on the patient's
nervous system.
Dettol is an antiseptic, a mixture of chloroxylenol and terpineol, applied to living tissue to
kill microorganisms.
∴ equanil.
